title: Water main breaks avoided

blocks.text: A water utility renews old cast-iron mains. Its asset team models each main's breaks with a Weibull curve, the way GridCap models failures: `breaks(age, beta, eta, years)` (given) is the expected number of breaks between ages `age` and `age + years` if the main is only repaired when it breaks. One break leaves `households` households without water for `hours` hours.

A renewal of **depth** `depth` makes the main as old as `(1 - depth)` times its age when the renewed main goes into service: 1 is a new pipe, 0.5 a relining. The work starts in year `start` and takes `duration` whole years (0 for a job finished within its first year), so the renewed main is in service from `start + duration`. Until then the old main keeps aging and breaking. `main.age` is its age in `first_year`, the first year of the plan, and benefits are counted over a window of `window` years from `first_year`.

Write `benefit(main, depth, start, duration, first_year, window)` in `mains.py`, returning the expected breaks avoided within the window and the household-hours without water they would have cost: `{"breaks": ..., "household_hours": ...}`. Work that goes into service at or after the end of the window avoids nothing.
Write the formula for the breaks avoided before you code it: which age goes in, and how many years are left? About eight lines.

cases.says: a replacement finished at once avoids the breaks and household-hours worked out by hand
a relining of depth 0.5 avoids the breaks of the years it takes away
a later start counts fewer years of benefit, on a main that has aged meanwhile
benefits are counted from the year the renewed main is in service, not from the start of work
the main's age at renewal includes the years of work as well as the wait
work that ends after the window avoids nothing, and never a negative amount
